newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: tough first lady for U.S. diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: tough first lady for U.S. diplomacy.

text.p: Cautious but plain-spoken, warm but tough, Madeleine Albright, nominated to be the next U.S. secretary of state, has become the Clinton administration's exponent of hard-hitting diplomacy.

"They have created a puppet show and called it a government," Albright, Washington's ambassador to the United Nations since 1993, said of Haiti's military dictators during a 1994 U.N. Security Council meeting. "You can depart voluntarily and soon, or you can depart involuntarily and soon," she said in issuing the U.S. ultimatum to the junta.

And when Cuban jet fighters downed two unarmed Miami-based planes in 1996, she told reporters, "This is not cojones, this is cowardice," using a Spanish vulgarity synonymous with macho male bravery, which the Cuban pilots had shouted.

Albright, whose nomination to the secretary of state was announced by President Bill Clinton on Thursday, will need all her toughness when she steps up as the first woman to hold this senior Cabinet post.

Born in Prague 59 years ago, she says her political life was moulded by the diplomatic appeasement of Adolf Hitler at Munich and by the experience of bomb shelters in London where her family fled the Nazi invasion.

"There are those who repeat the historical error of believing that America can isolate itself from the rest of the world," she has said. "Distant problems, if left unattended, will one day come home to America."

As an expert in eastern Europe, she made news with a leaked 1993 memo telling Clinton to initiate punitive NATO air strikes to destroy the Bosnian Serbs' heavy weapons. Many credit the memo with laying the groundwork for U.S. policy that led to bombing and then to the 1995 Balkan peace talks.

Critics say Albright, already a member of Clinton's Cabinet as U.N. ambassador, often seems to be improvising U.S. policy on the spot. But insiders say she coordinates each word with Washington and reads notes even during informal council sessions, where she is the only female ambassador.
Like her Security Council performances, Albright's encounters with the press are tightly controlled. She seldom chats informally with reporters, as many other U.N. envoys do.

At the United Nations, she has had her successes and been the subject of biting criticism -- and never more so than just a few weeks ago when she cast the U.S. veto of a second-term for Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali while her 14 Security Council colleagues voted for him.

She has also had to cope with a mounting U.S. debt of more than $1 billion to the world body, which undercuts her criticism of Boutros-Ghali for not spending enough time on reforming the United Nations.
"When I have tried to focus my colleagues on the reform agenda, I have found instead that the United States has become the agenda," she told the Council on Foreign Relations.
Unlike her predecessor Thomas Pickering, known as a diplomat's diplomat, Albright is attuned to politics and has campaigned around the country and tirelessly shuttles between Washington and New York.

Those U.N. envoys who know her well consider her warm and personable. But even critics admit her speeches get right to the point and are a refreshing change from the familiar blandness and evasions of diplomatic rhetoric.

She began her U.N. job by promoting "assertive multilateralism," saying the United States could not be the world's policeman. Then came Somalia, where 18 U.S. soldiers were killed and Washington became wary of peacekeeping.

Born Maria Jana Korbelova in Prague on May 15, 1937, Albright spent the war years with her family in London. She attended school in Switzerland at age 10 and acquired the name Madeleine. Her father, a diplomat and academic, got a teaching job in Denver, where she spent most of her adolescence.
She attended exclusive Wellesley College in Massachusetts, got a doctorate from Columbia University and speaks Czech, Polish, Russian and French as well as English.
Albright joined the staff of Senator Edmund Muskie, a Maine Democrat, in 1976 and two years later became a member of President Jimmy Carter's National Security Council staff.
She was a foreign policy adviser in the presidential campaigns of Walter Mondale and Michael Dukakis, drubbed by Ronald Reagan and George Bush in 1984 and 1988 respectively.
Divorced from newspaper heir Joseph Albright, she has raised three daughters.
